cues.text: Oh good morning. You must be James. I’m Beth Cartwright – please call me Beth.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Thank you.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Now as this is your first tutorial since you started on the Scandinavian Studies course, I’d like to find out something about you. Why did you decide to take this course?
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Well, my mother is Danish, and although we always lived in England, she used to talk about her home a lot, and that made me want to visit Denmark. We hardly ever did, though – my mother usually went on her own. But whenever her relations or friends were in England they always came to see us.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: I see. So I assume you already speak Danish, one of the languages you’ll be studying.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: I can get by when I talk to people, though I’m not terribly accurate.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Now you probably know that you’ll spend the third year of the course abroad. Have you had any thoughts about that?
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: I’m really looking forward to it. And although Denmark seems the obvious place to go, because of my family connections, I’d love to spend the time in Iceland.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Oh, I’m sure it can be arranged. Do you have any plans for when you graduate? A lot of students go on to take a master’s degree.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: I think the four years of the undergraduate course will be enough for me. I’m interested in journalism, and I quite like the idea of moving to Scandinavia and writing for magazines. I’d find that more creative than translating, which I suppose most graduates do.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: OK. Now how are you finding the courses you’re taking this term, James?
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Well, I’m really enjoying the one on Swedish cinema.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: That’ll continue next term, but the one on Scandinavian literature that’s running at the moment will be replaced by more specialised courses. Oh, and by the way, if you’re interested in watching Danish television programmes – there’s going to be a course on that the term after next.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: That sounds good.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Have you started thinking about the literature paper that you have to write in the next few weeks?
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Yes, my first choice would be to do something on the Icelandic sagas.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Hmm. The trouble with that is that a lot of people choose that topic, and it can be difficult to get hold of the books you’ll need. Why not leave that for another time?
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: You might find modern novels or 19th century playwrights interesting.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: I’ve read or seen several plays in translation, so that would be a good idea.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Fine. I’ll put you down for that topic.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Right. So what would you advise me to aim at in the paper?
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: First I suggest you avoid taking one writer and going into a great deal of detail. That approach certainly has its place, but I think you first need to get an understanding of the literature in the context of the society in which it was produced – who it was written for, how it was published, and so on. I also think that’s more fruitful than placing it within the history of the genre.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: OK, that sounds reasonable.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Could I ask for some advice about writing the paper I’m working on about the Vikings? I have to do that this week, and I’m a bit stuck.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Of course. Have you decided yet what to write about?
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: No, I haven’t. There’s so much that seems interesting – Viking settlement in other countries, trade, mythology …
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: Well, what I suggest is that you read an assignment a student wrote last year, which is kept in the library. It’s short and well focused, and I’m sure you’ll find it helpful. I’ll give you the details in a moment. Textbooks usually cover so many topics, it can be very difficult to choose just one.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: OK. I’ve got a DVD of the film about the Vikings that came out earlier this year. Should I watch that again?
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: If it’s the one I am thinking of, hmm, I’d ignore it – it’s more fantasy than reality. But I’ve got a recording of a documentary that you should watch. It makes some interesting and provocative points, which I think will help you to focus your topic.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: So then should I work out an outline?
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Yes. Just headings for different sections, at this stage. And then you should start looking for suitable articles and books to draw on, and take notes which you organise according to those headings.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: I see.
cues.speaker: BETH

cues.text: Then put short phrases and sentences as bullet points under each heading. Make sure that this skeleton makes sense and flows properly, before writing up the paper in full.
cues.speaker: JAMES

cues.text: OK. Thanks, that’s very helpful.
cues.speaker: BETH
